question_interpretation: Asks for the general requirements for informed consent in 21 CFR 50.20 and the basic (and, by extension, additional) elements of informed consent in 50.25.

issues.detail: J lists only some of the 50.20 general requirements: it omits that consent may be sought only under circumstances giving the subject/LAR sufficient opportunity to consider participation and minimizing the possibility of coercion or undue influence, and that consent may come from the subject's legally authorized representative.

50.20 is expressly subject to the exceptions in 50.22 (IRB waiver/alteration for minimal-risk investigations, added 88 FR 88248, Dec. 21, 2023), 50.23 and 50.24; J does not mention that the general requirement has exceptions.
50.25(c) requires the ClinicalTrials.gov statement for applicable clinical trials; J lists only basic and additional elements.
'Comprehension' is not regulatory wording; 50.20 requires information in language understandable to the subject or representative.

explanation: G is correct: 50.20 sets the general requirements and 50.25 the elements. J is right as far as it goes, but its list of general requirements leaves out the coercion/undue-influence and opportunity-to-consider condition, the LAR route, and the express exceptions (50.22-50.24). It also leaves out the mandatory 50.25(c) statement. These omissions are material for a question about 'general requirements'.
proposed_corrected_answer: 50.20: no investigator may involve a human subject without the legally effective informed consent of the subject or the subject's legally authorized representative, except as provided in 50.22, 50.23 and 50.24. Consent may be sought only under circumstances that give sufficient opportunity to consider whether to participate and that minimize the possibility of coercion or undue influence. Information must be in language understandable to the subject/representative. No exculpatory language waiving the subject's legal rights or releasing the investigator, sponsor, institution or agents from liability for negligence. 50.25(a) basic elements (8): research statement/purpose/duration/procedures/experimental procedures; foreseeable risks; expected benefits; alternatives; confidentiality incl. possible FDA inspection; for more than minimal risk, compensation/medical treatment for injury; contacts for questions and research-related injury; voluntary participation, no penalty, may discontinue. 50.25(b) additional elements (6) when appropriate. 50.25(c) ClinicalTrials.gov statement for applicable clinical trials. (Documentation: 50.27.)

question_interpretation: Asks the conditions under which a clinical investigation may proceed under the exception from informed consent for emergency research (21 CFR 50.24).

issues.detail: J omits several 50.24(a) findings the IRB must make and document: concurrence of a licensed physician not otherwise participating; the investigation could not practicably be carried out without the waiver; a therapeutic window defined, with commitment to try to contact a LAR within it; IRB-approved consent procedures and document plus family-member objection procedures; an independent data monitoring committee.

50.24(d), 312.20(c) and 812.20(a)(4): the protocol must be under a separate IND/IDE and may not proceed without FDA's prior written authorization (FDA decision within 30 days). Not in J or G (312.20(c)/812.20(a)(4) not cited).
50.24(b) notification of the subject/LAR/family at the earliest feasible opportunity, 50.24(c) 3-year IRB record retention, 50.24(e) IRB disapproval findings; sponsor duties in 312.54/812.47.

explanation: 50.24 is the right governing section and J's items (life-threatening situation, consent not feasible, prospect of direct benefit, IRB findings, community consultation, public disclosure) are supported. J omits material conditions to proceed: physician concurrence, independent DMC, the therapeutic-window LAR-contact commitment, and the separate IND/IDE requirement with FDA's prior written authorization (50.24(d); 312.20(c); 812.20(a)(4)).

issues.detail: 50.56 (wards): wards may be enrolled in 50.53/50.54 investigations only if related to their ward status or conducted where most child subjects are not wards, and the IRB must require an advocate for each ward. Within the cited range but absent from J.

question_interpretation: Asks how long GLP study records and specimens must be retained (58.195) and, per J, the archive requirements.

issues.detail: J gives no retention periods. 58.195(b) requires retention for whichever of these is shortest: at least 2 years after FDA approves the application the study supported (not for IND/IDE studies); at least 5 years after the results are submitted to FDA; or at least 2 years after study completion/termination if never submitted. 'Tied to the type of application' misdescribes a rule keyed to approval, submission or completion dates and resolved by 'whichever is shortest'.
J requires 'archive requirements' but G cites only 58.195. Archive requirements (orderly storage, minimizing deterioration, responsible individual, restricted access, indexing) are in 58.190(b)-(e).

58.195(c): fragile wet specimens/samples kept only as long as quality affords evaluation. 58.195(h): if the facility goes out of business, materials go to the sponsor's archives and FDA is notified in writing. 58.195(d)-(f): QA, training and equipment records.

explanation: 58.195 is the right retention section, but J states no periods and omits the 'whichever is shortest' rule, which is the substance of an Advanced retention question. J also invokes archive requirements without citing 58.190, where they live.
proposed_corrected_answer: Under 58.195(b), documentation records, raw data and specimens are retained in the archives for whichever is shortest: (1) at least 2 years after FDA approves the research or marketing permit the study supported (does not apply to IND/IDE-supporting studies, which fall under (b)(2)); (2) at least 5 years after the study results are submitted to FDA in support of an application; (3) otherwise, at least 2 years after the study is completed, terminated or discontinued. Fragile wet specimens and test/control article samples are kept only as long as their quality affords evaluation (58.195(c)). QA master schedule/protocol copies/inspection records, training summaries and equipment records follow the same periods (58.195(d)-(f)). True copies are allowed (58.195(g)). If the facility goes out of business, records go to the sponsor's archives with written notice to FDA (58.195(h)). Archives: orderly storage and expedient retrieval, conditions minimizing deterioration, an individual responsible, authorized-only access, and indexing (58.190(b)-(e)). 58.195 does not supersede other retention rules (58.195(a)).

question_interpretation: Asks which farms and which produce are covered by the Produce Safety Rule (Part 112) and what exemptions/exclusions apply.

issues.detail: The 'produce rarely consumed raw' exclusion that J requires is in 21 CFR 112.2(a)(1), which G does not cite. 112.2 also excludes produce grown for personal or same-farm consumption and produce that is not a RAC (112.2(a)(2)-(3)), and provides the commercial-processing exemption with disclosure and annual written assurances (112.2(b)).

Monetary thresholds should be stated: a covered farm averages more than $25,000 in annual produce sales over the previous 3 years (112.4(a)). The qualified exemption requires average annual food sales under $500,000 and sales to qualified end-users exceeding sales to all other buyers (112.5(a)). Both are inflation-adjusted from a 2011 baseline. Qualified-exempt farms have modified requirements (112.6) and records (112.7), and the exemption can be withdrawn (subpart R).
Because G omits 112.2, the key cites no home for one of its own required elements.

explanation: 112.1, 112.4 and 112.5 are correct for covered produce, covered farms and the qualified exemption. The rarely-consumed-raw exclusion and the other produce exclusions and exemptions are in 112.2, which G omits. J says 'monetary thresholds' without the $25,000 / $500,000 figures.
proposed_corrected_answer: Covered produce: produce that is a RAC, domestic or imported, including the listed fruits and vegetables, mixes, mushrooms, sprouts and herbs (112.1), unless excluded. Not covered (112.2(a)): produce on the exhaustive rarely-consumed-raw list; produce for personal or same-farm consumption; produce that is not a RAC. Exempt subject to conditions (112.2(b)): produce that receives commercial processing that adequately reduces pathogens, with disclosure and annual written assurances and records. Covered farm (112.4(a)): average annual produce sales over the previous 3 years of more than $25,000 (inflation-adjusted, 2011 baseline). Not covered if the farm meets 112.5 and the exemption has not been withdrawn (112.4(b)). Qualified exemption (112.5): average annual food sales under $500,000 (inflation-adjusted) and sales to qualified end-users exceeding sales to all other buyers over the previous 3 years. Modified requirements apply (112.6, 112.7), and the exemption may be withdrawn (subpart R).

question_interpretation: Asks the pH-control requirements for acidified foods under Part 114.

issues.detail: J requires 'required records' but G does not cite 114.100. 114.90 lists methods that 'may be used'; most of its procedural text is advisory ('should'). The mandatory method choice is in 114.80(a)(2). Related: 108.25 (registration and process filing for acidified foods).

explanation: 114.80 is the core section, and J's pH 4.6 and monitoring elements are supported. J requires records but G omits 114.100, the records section. The pH-deviation rule (114.89) and the potentiometric-method requirement above pH 4.0 are omitted.
proposed_corrected_answer: Acidified foods (aw > 0.85, finished equilibrium pH 4.6 or below; 114.3(b)) must be made so that a finished equilibrium pH of 4.6 or lower is achieved within the time set in the scheduled process and maintained. They must also be thermally processed (or preserved) to destroy vegetative cells (114.80(a)(1)). Sufficient control, including frequent testing and recording, must keep finished equilibrium pH no higher than 4.6. If finished pH is above 4.0, it is measured potentiometrically and in-process titration/colorimetry is related to it; at 4.0 or below any suitable method may be used (114.80(a)(2)). Methods are described in 114.90. If the process deviates or finished pH exceeds 4.6, the processor must fully reprocess, have the lot evaluated by a competent processing authority, or destroy it, and record the actions (114.89). Records of processing and production including pH measurements, deviations and initial distribution are kept 3 years (114.100(b)-(e)). Registration and process filing: 108.25.
